title: 大智度論
text: 佛告須菩提：「三千大千世界中諸惡魔皆愁毒，如箭入心，各於其坐不能自安。須菩提！菩薩摩訶薩能如是行般若波羅蜜，是時一切世間天及人、阿修羅不能得其便令其憂惱。須菩提！以是故，菩薩摩訶薩欲得阿耨多羅三藐三菩提，當行是般若波羅蜜！菩薩摩訶薩行般若波羅蜜時，具足修檀波羅蜜、尸羅波羅蜜、羼提波羅蜜、毘梨耶波羅蜜、禪波羅蜜、般若波羅蜜。須菩提！菩薩摩訶薩行般若波羅蜜時，具足諸波羅蜜。」
A_soloOnly: The Buddha said to Subhūti, "In the three-thousand-fold great thousand-fold world system (tri-sāhasra-mahat-sāhasra-lokadhātu), all the evil demons are sorrowful and pained, as if an arrow had entered their hearts, and each is unable to remain at ease in his seat. Subhūti, when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva (great being) can practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñā-pāramitā) in this way, at that time all the gods, humans, and antigods (asura) in the entire world (sarva-loka) cannot find an opportunity to cause him worry or affliction. Subhūti, for this reason, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva who wishes to attain unsurpassed, perfect awakening (anuttara-samyaksambodhi) should practice this perfection of wisdom. When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he fully cultivates the perfection of generosity (dāna-pāramitā), the perfection of morality (śīla-pāramitā), the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā), the perfection of effort (vīrya-pāramitā), the perfection of meditation (dhyāna-pāramitā), and the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti, when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he fully possesses all the perfections (sarva-pāramitā)."
B_equalFocus:
The perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) is not truly perceived, nor is the phenomenon (dharma) by which one perceives the perfection of wisdom truly perceived. The same applies to the perfection of meditation (dhyāna-pāramitā) and the perfection of generosity (dāna-pāramitā). In this way, even enlightenment (bodhi) is not truly perceived, nor is the phenomenon by which one perceives enlightenment truly perceived. Subhūti, because a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not apprehend all phenomena in this way, he should practice the perfection of wisdom.

Subhūti, whenever a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom without apprehending all phenomena, at that time, Māra the Wicked One is pierced by the thorn of grief. Subhūti, for example, just as a person whose parents have died is pierced by the thorn of grief and suffers a great thorn of grief, likewise, Subhūti, at the time when a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells without being separated from the state of the perfection of wisdom, all the wicked Māras who dwell in the tri-sāhasra-mahat-sāhasra-lokadhātu are pierced by an unbearable thorn of grief and cannot find comfort on their own seats. A bodhisattva mahāsattva who dwells in this way cannot be seized or harmed by the world, including its gods, humans, and asuras.

Subhūti, therefore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to fully awaken to the unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment (anuttara-samyaksambodhi) should dwell in the state of the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti, in this way, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom without apprehending all phenomena, Māra the Wicked One is pierced by a great thorn of grief. By dwelling in the state of the perfection of wisdom, a bodhisattva mahāsattva fulfills the cultivation of the perfection of generosity.

Then the Venerable Subhūti asked the Blessed One, "Blessed One, is it only one wicked Māra who is pierced by a great thorn of grief, or are all the wicked Māras who dwell in the tri-sāhasra-mahat-sāhasra-lokadhātu pierced by a great thorn of grief and unable to find joy on their own seats?"

The Blessed One replied, "Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he fulfills the cultivation of all the perfections (pāramitā)."

Subhūti, for example, if a person’s parents have died, would one wicked Māra be pierced by an unbearable thorn of grief, or would all the wicked Māras in the tri-sāhasra-mahat-sāhasra-lokadhātu be pierced by an unbearable thorn of grief?

The Blessed One replied, "They are pierced by the thorn of grief; they are possessed of an unbearable thorn of grief. Subhūti, in the same way, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom without apprehending all phenomena, the wicked Māras are pierced by the thorn of grief and are possessed of an unbearable thorn of grief."

Subhūti asked, "All the wicked Māras who exist in the tri-sāhasra-mahat-sāhasra-lokadhātu are pierced by an unbearable thorn of grief and do not wish to sit on their own seats. A bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices in this way cannot be seized or turned back by the world, including its gods, humans, and asuras; they cannot find his depth."

The Blessed One replied, "Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom without apprehending all phenomena, the wicked Māras are pierced by the thorn of grief and are possessed of an unbearable thorn of grief. All the wicked Māras who exist in the tri-sāhasra-mahat-sāhasra-lokadhātu are pierced by an unbearable thorn of grief."
C_chineseFocus: The Buddha said to Subhūti, "In the tri-sāhasra-mahat-sāhasra-lokadhātu, all the wicked Māras are filled with sorrow and poison, as if an arrow had entered their hearts, and each is unable to remain at ease in his seat. Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva can practice the prajñāpāramitā in this way, at that time, the gods, humans, and asuras of the entire sarva-loka cannot find an opportunity to cause him worry or affliction. Subhūti, for this reason, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to attain anuttara-samyaksambodhi should practice this prajñāpāramitā. When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, he fully cultivates the dāna-pāramitā, the śīla-pāramitā, the kṣānti-pāramitā, the vīrya-pāramitā, the dhyāna-pāramitā, and the prajñāpāramitā. Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, he fully possesses all the pāramitās."

title: 大智度論
text: 佛告須菩提：「色如相，受、想、行、識如相，乃至涅槃如相，是阿耨多羅三藐三菩提。是如相亦不增不減。須菩提！是菩薩摩訶薩不離般若波羅蜜，常觀是如法，不見有增有減。以是因緣故，須菩提！不可說義無增無減，檀波羅蜜亦不增不減，乃至十八不共法亦不增不減。須菩提！菩薩摩訶薩以是不增不減法故，應般若波羅蜜行。」
A_soloOnly: The Buddha said to Subhūti: "The form is the nature of suchness (tathatā), and feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are the nature of suchness, up to and including the nature of suchness of nirvāṇa; this is the unexcelled perfect awakening (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi). This nature of suchness neither increases nor decreases. Subhūti, this Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva does not depart from the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), constantly contemplating this dharma of suchness, and does not perceive any increase or decrease. Because of this causal condition (pratyaya), Subhūti, the inexpressible (anabhilāpya) meaning neither increases nor decreases, the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramitā) neither increases nor decreases, and up to and including the eighteen exclusive qualities (āveṇika-dharma) neither increase nor decrease. Subhūti, because of this dharma of non-increase and non-decrease, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva should practice the perfection of wisdom."
B_equalFocus:
For a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), cultivating the perfection of wisdom, and engaging in the perfection of wisdom, it does not occur to one who is skilled in means, "I am increasing through the perfection of wisdom," or "I am increasing through the perfection of meditative concentration." Rather, one thinks, "This which is the perfection of generosity is merely a name." While practicing the perfection of generosity, one dedicates those mental states, those arisings of mind, and those roots of goodness toward unsurpassed, perfectly complete enlightenment (samyaksambodhi), and one dedicates them just as unsurpassed, perfectly complete enlightenment is. It is the same when practicing the perfection of wisdom: one dedicates those mental states, those arisings of mind, and those roots of goodness toward unsurpassed, perfectly complete enlightenment, and one dedicates them just as unsurpassed, perfectly complete enlightenment is.

"Subhūti, what is unsurpassed, perfectly complete enlightenment?"

"Bhagavant, just as the suchness (tathatā) of all phenomena is, so too is unsurpassed, perfectly complete enlightenment."

"Subhūti, what is the suchness of all phenomena that is unsurpassed, perfectly complete enlightenment?"

"Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is skilled in means is practicing the perfection of wisdom, cultivating the perfection of wisdom, and exerting oneself in the perfection of wisdom, it does not occur to one, 'I am increasing through the perfection of wisdom,' nor does one think, 'I am increasing through the perfection of meditative concentration, the perfection of perseverance, the perfection of patience, the perfection of ethical discipline, or the perfection of generosity.' Rather, one thinks, 'This is merely a name,' thinking of the perfection of generosity, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of perseverance, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom as merely names. While practicing the perfection of generosity, one dedicates those mental states, those arisings of mind, and those roots of goodness toward unsurpassed, perfectly complete enlightenment, and one dedicates them just as unsurpassed, perfectly complete enlightenment is."

"Bhagavant, what is unsurpassed, perfectly complete enlightenment?"

"Subhūti, just as the suchness of form is, so too is unsurpassed, perfectly complete enlightenment. Just as the suchness of feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness is, so too is unsurpassed, perfectly complete enlightenment. Just as the suchness of all phenomena is, so too is unsurpassed, perfectly complete enlightenment. Just as the suchness of all-knowledge is, so too is unsurpassed, perfectly complete enlightenment. Just as the suchness of nirvāṇa is, so too is unsurpassed, perfectly complete enlightenment."

Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is not separated from the perfection of wisdom dwells constantly in this way, and one does not perceive any phenomenon as increasing or decreasing. Subhūti, for that which is inexpressible (anabhilāpya), there is neither increase nor decrease. Thus, Subhūti, for the perfection of generosity, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of perseverance, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom, there is neither increase nor decrease.
C_chineseFocus: The Buddha said to Subhūti, "The suchness (tathatā) of form, the suchness of feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness, up to and including the suchness of nirvana, is the unsurpassed, perfectly complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyaksambodhi). This suchness neither increases nor decreases. Subhūti, this bodhisattva mahāsattva does not depart from the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā); he constantly contemplates this dharma of suchness and does not see any increase or decrease. For this reason, Subhūti, the inexpressible (anabhilāpya) meaning has no increase or decrease; the perfection of generosity (dāna-pāramitā) also neither increases nor decreases, and even the eighteen exclusive dharmas (āveṇika) neither increase nor decrease. Subhūti, because of this dharma of no increase and no decrease, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice the perfection of wisdom."

title: 大智度論
text: 佛言：「不與不善法合，不與善法合；不與世間法合，不與出世間法合；不與有漏法合，不與無漏法合；不與有罪法合，不與無罪法合；不與有為法合，不與無為法合。何以故？般若波羅蜜不為得諸法故生，以是故於諸法無所合。」
A_soloOnly: The Buddha said: "It does not combine with unwholesome phenomena (akuśala-dharma), and it does not combine with wholesome phenomena (kuśala-dharma); it does not combine with worldly phenomena (laukika-dharma), and it does not combine with supramundane phenomena (lokottara-dharma); it does not combine with phenomena subject to influxes (āsrava-dharma), and it does not combine with phenomena free from influxes (anāsrava-dharma); it does not combine with faulty phenomena (anavadya-dharma), and it does not combine with faultless phenomena (anavadya-dharma); it does not combine with conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta-dharma), and it does not combine with unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta-dharma). Why is this? The perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) does not arise for the sake of attaining phenomena (dharma); for this reason, it does not combine with any phenomena."
B_equalFocus:
Then the venerable Subhūti said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, how does the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) bestow any dharma? It is because form is without volitional construction (saṃskāra), without arising, without essence, without origination, without apprehension, and without destruction; and up to all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā), it is without volitional construction, without arising, without essence, without origination, without apprehension, and without destruction—that one should practice the perfection of wisdom. This is what is meant by not engaging in volitional construction regarding all dharmas. Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom practiced in this way does not bestow any dharma whatsoever. When one does not bestow any dharma, that is when one enters the count of the perfection of wisdom. It does not bestow unwholesome dharmas (akuśala-dharma), nor does it bestow blameless dharmas (anavadya), nor those with impurities (āsrava), nor those without impurities (anāsrava-dharma), nor conditioned dharmas (saṃskṛta-dharma), nor unconditioned dharmas (asaṃskṛta-dharma), nor those that are defiled, nor those that are undefiled, nor worldly dharmas (laukika), nor supramundane dharmas (lokottara-dharma), nor those that are associated with defilement, nor those that are purified, nor those of cyclic existence (saṃsāra), nor those of nirvana. The perfection of wisdom does not abide by way of apprehending any dharma whatsoever; therefore, it does not bestow any dharma."

"What dharma does it not bestow?" Then the venerable Subhūti said to the Blessed One: "Subhūti, because form is without volitional construction, without arising, without apprehension, and without destruction, one should practice the perfection of wisdom in this way. Likewise, from feeling, perception, and volitional formations up to consciousness and all-knowledge, because they are without volitional construction, without arising, without apprehension, and without destruction, one should practice the perfection of wisdom in this way."

"If the perfection of wisdom is practiced in this way, what dharma does one attain?"

"Likewise, one does not attain worldly dharmas, nor supramundane dharmas, nor dharmas with impurities, nor dharmas without impurities, nor blameworthy dharmas, nor blameless dharmas, nor conditioned dharmas, nor unconditioned dharmas. One does not attain any dharma whatsoever; therefore, it enters the count of what is called the perfection of wisdom. One does not attain wholesome dharmas (kuśala-dharma) nor unwholesome dharmas. Subhūti, in this way, the perfection of wisdom does not abide by way of apprehending any dharmas; therefore, it does not attain any dharma whatsoever."
C_chineseFocus: The Buddha said: "It does not combine with unwholesome dharmas (akuśala-dharma), nor does it combine with wholesome dharmas (kuśala-dharma); it does not combine with worldly dharmas (loka), nor does it combine with supramundane dharmas (lokottara-dharma); it does not combine with tainted dharmas (āsrava), nor does it combine with untainted dharmas (anāsrava-dharma); it does not combine with faulty dharmas, nor does it combine with faultless dharmas (anavadya); it does not combine with conditioned dharmas (saṃskṛta-dharma), nor does it combine with unconditioned dharmas (asaṃskṛta-dharma). For what reason? The perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) does not arise for the sake of attaining any dharmas; for this reason, it does not combine with any dharmas."

title: 雜阿含經
text: 「若諸善法生，一切皆明為根本，明集、明生、明起。明，於善、不善法如實知者，罪、無罪，親近、不親近，卑法、勝法，穢污、白淨，有分別、無分別，緣起、非緣起悉如實知，如實知者，是則正見。正見者，能起正志、正語、正業、正命、正方便、正念、正定。正定起已，聖弟子得正解脫貪、恚、癡，貪、恚、癡解脫已，是聖弟子得正智見：『我生已盡，梵行已立，所作已作，自知不受後有。』」
A_soloOnly: “If any wholesome states (kuśala-dharma) arise, all of them have clarity (vidyā) as their root, clarity as their gathering, clarity as their arising, and clarity as their manifestation. Clarity is the knowing things as they really are (yathābhūtam prajñā) regarding wholesome and unwholesome states (akuśala-dharma): knowing as they really are what is blameworthy and blameless, what should be cultivated and what should not be cultivated, what is base and what is superior, what is defiled and what is pure, what is with conceptualization (vikalpa) and what is without conceptualization (nirvikalpa), and what is dependently originated and what is not dependently originated. Knowing things as they really are is right view. Through right view, one is able to give rise to right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort (upāya), right mindfulness, and right concentration. Once right concentration has arisen, the noble disciple (ārya-śrāvaka) attains right liberation (vimokṣa) from greed, hatred, and delusion. Once liberated from greed, hatred, and delusion, this noble disciple attains right knowledge and vision: ‘Birth for me has been eradicated, the holy life (brahmacarya) has been established, what had to be done (kṛtya) has been done, I myself know that there will be no receiving of any further existence.’”
B_equalFocus: If any wholesome states (kuśala-dharma) arise, all of them have clarity (vidyā) as their root, clarity as their gathering, clarity as their arising, and clarity as their inception. Clarity is knowing wholesome and unwholesome states (akuśala-dharma) as they truly are (yathābhūtam prajñā): knowing what is blameworthy and blameless, what is to be cultivated and what is not to be cultivated, what is inferior and what is superior, what is defiled and what is pure, what is with conceptualization (vikalpa) and what is without conceptualization (nirvikalpa), and what is dependent on conditions and what is not dependent on conditions—all this one knows as it truly is. Knowing as it truly is, this is right view. From right view, one can give rise to right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort (upāya), right mindfulness, and right concentration. Once right concentration has arisen, the noble disciple (ārya-śrāvaka) attains right liberation (vimokṣa) from greed, hatred, and delusion. Once liberated from greed, hatred, and delusion, this noble disciple attains right knowledge and vision: "Birth for me has been eradicated, the holy life (brahmacarya) has been established, what had to be done has been done, I myself know that there will be no receiving of any further existence."
C_chineseFocus: "If any wholesome states (kuśala-dharma) arise, all of them have clarity as their root, clarity as their gathering, clarity as their arising, and clarity as their manifestation. Clarity is that which knows wholesome and unwholesome states as they really are (yathābhūtam prajñā); it knows as they really are what is blameworthy and blameless, what is to be cultivated and what is not to be cultivated, what is inferior and what is superior, what is defiled and what is pure, what has discrimination (vikalpa) and what is without discrimination (avikalpa), and what is dependent on conditions and what is not dependent on conditions. One who knows as they really are is possessed of right view. One who has right view is able to give rise to right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort (upāya), right mindfulness, and right concentration. Once right concentration has arisen, the noble disciple (ārya-śrāvaka) attains right liberation from greed, hatred, and delusion. Once liberated from greed, hatred, and delusion, this noble disciple attains right knowledge and vision: 'Birth for me has been eradicated, the holy life (brahmacarya) has been established, what had to be done has been done, I myself know that there will be no receiving of any further existence.'"
